title: Beha'alotcha: until it rises alone (Numbers 8:2)
hookLine: Rashi: Aaron holds the light to the wick until the flame rises by itself

cards: A birthday cake, a version from the window, one match. You touch the match to the wick. The wick blackens, smokes, takes a tiny blue bead of flame.
Pull the match away too soon and it dies. So you wait, holding steady, until the flame stands up on its own and doesn't need you anymore. Then you let go.
That small, patient moment is how the commentator Rashi explains the word this week's portion is named for, and it becomes a picture of what a teacher does.

teach.b: God tells Moses to speak to Aaron: "When thou lightest the lamps," the seven lamps of the menorah shall give light toward its front. In Hebrew, when thou lightest is beha'alotcha, and it doesn't literally say light.
It says when you raise up, when you make it go up. Rashi asks why. His answer, from the ancient rabbis: because the flame goes upward.

teach.h: HOLD IT TILL IT RISES ALONE.
teach.b: Aaron must hold the light to each wick until the flame rises by itself. Rashi's second comment connects to yesterday. Why does this section come right after the leaders' twelve gifts?
Because, the midrash says, Aaron felt left out. Every tribe had a leader at the dedication, and his tribe, Levi, brought nothing. So God told him: yours is greater than theirs.
They brought gifts once. You will light and tend the lamps.

teach.h: A GIFT IS ONCE. A FLAME IS KEPT.
teach.b: A gift is given and done; a flame has to be kept.
Then the verse says simply: and Aaron did so. Rashi reads that as praise: he didn't change a thing, day after day. The image is often borrowed for teaching.
You don't light someone by grabbing their wick and holding it forever, or by touching it once and walking away.
You stay close, steady, until the light is theirs. Then you step back, and the flame keeps going up.

how: Beha'alotcha is read in early summer; Rashi's comments on its first verse, that the flame must be held until it rises by itself, and that Aaron's tending of the lamps outshone the leaders' gifts, are often taught as a picture of teaching and patience.

practice: Think of someone just starting something: a kid learning to cook, a new coworker, a friend trying to quit something, a student stuck on a problem.
Ask honestly whether you pull the match away too soon, or hold it there so long it never becomes theirs. Picture one way to stay close a little longer, and one way to let go a little sooner.

wordCard.voice: Beha'alotcha. When you raise up: the lamp held until it burns alone. This week: cover what's holy, counting is lifting, repay and add a fifth, a vow for a season, the priests' blessing, each gift counted in full, and now this.
